chunks: What is aliasing?. The question: What is aliasing?
Aliasing happens when you sample a signal too slowly. Frequencies above half the sample rate do not simply vanish.
They fold back and appear as lower frequencies in your data, and from the samples alone you cannot tell the fake from a real low-frequency signal.
So it must be prevented before sampling, with an analog filter.
You have seen it in films: a car's wheel seems to turn slowly, or even backward. The camera takes pictures at a fixed rate, too slow to follow the fast spokes.
Each frame shows the spokes nearly where they were, so the brain reads a slow, false motion. A slow sampler gives a fast signal the same illusion.
The apparent frequency rises with the true frequency up to the Nyquist frequency (500 hertz), then folds back down, rising and falling again every 500 hertz.
A true frequency of 1000 hertz (a multiple of fs) lands on DC. The only unambiguous region is 0 to 500 hertz.
Drag fs down to 750 hertz and the 900 hertz tone now folds to 150 hertz instead of 100 hertz, so changing the sampling rate changes what an alias looks like.
Sample rate: how many measurements are taken per second. Nyquist frequency: half the sample rate, the highest frequency that can be represented.
Alias: the false lower frequency that a too-fast signal turns into. Anti-alias filter: a filter before the converter that removes frequencies above the Nyquist frequency.
Switching ripple: a small repeating wobble on a supply voltage, made by a power circuit that switches on and off rapidly.
The apparent frequency is the distance from the signal's frequency to the nearest multiple of the sample rate.
At 1000 samples per second, a 900 hertz sine looks like 100 hertz, a 1200 hertz tone like 200 hertz, and a 2300 hertz tone like 300 hertz.
In hardware: a converter (ADC) samples a supply at 100 kS/s, and the supply has 500 kilohertz ripple.
500 kilohertz is exactly 5 times the sample rate, so the ripple looks like 0 hertz, a constant offset. If it drifts to 480 kilohertz, it appears as a 20 kilohertz tone.
A quick test: change the sample rate slightly. Real signals stay put and aliases move. That is the whole idea.
"Aliasing is when a signal above half the sample rate folds back and appears as a lower frequency in the sampled data.
The apparent frequency is the distance to the nearest multiple of fs: a 900 hertz tone sampled at 1 kilohertz looks like 100 hertz.
It's irreversible, so you prevent it with an analog anti-alias low-pass before the ADC, often with oversampling.
It also folds noise in, and a quick test is to change fs: aliases move, real signals don't."
